Table 4A reports AI versus No AI, CLM mean ± SE: chatbot benefits 1.99 ±.18 versus 1.88 ±.06; medical benefits 1.90* ±.23 versus 2.09 ±.06; chatbot risks 1.89 ±.11 versus 1.87 ±.03; medical risks 1.96** ±.18 versus 1.75 ±.05; chatbot mitigations 1.86 ±.11 versus 1.87 ±.03; medical mitigations 1.89 ±.20 versus 1.80 ±.06. Retain the printed significance marks, including the medical-benefit AI cell (* p < .05) and medical-risk AI cell (** p < .01); the corresponding No AI cells have no stars.

corrections.form_value: No semantic-diversity result is recorded in outcomes or notes; Figure 14 is mentioned only in source.supplement.holds.
corrections.source_says: Record the supplementary semantic-distance result, or explicitly document its exclusion from assistance-effect outcomes. Figure 14 compares AI-generated with human-generated benefits, risks, and mitigations using Cosine Distance (1 - cosine similarity). All three panels print Mann-Whitney U: p < 0.05; the plotted AI-generated distributions have lower cosine distances. This is labeled as an output-origin comparison, not a comparison of AI-assisted versus unassisted human teams, so it does not establish an across_people assistance effect. If retained as an outcome, comparison_type should describe AI versus human output and question should be none unless the assistance contrast can be established. The embedding model, which outputs or pairs were compared, the observation unit, sample sizes, exact U statistics, numerical group summaries, and confidence intervals are not specified; leave these null.
corrections.quote: Semantic similarity for AI-generated vs. human-generated benefits (left), risks (middle), and mitigations (right).

confirmed: The source is arXiv:2604.27997v1, dated 30 April 2026, a FAccT 2026 manuscript; the PDF has 36 pages and includes Appendices A-H on pp. 21-36 (PDF p. 1 version stamp; pp. 21-36 appendices).

No random assignment of AI assistance is documented. Participants registered and were assigned to groups with balanced backgrounds; other / randomized not_stated and provisional core unclear / context none are warranted rather than a confirmed RCT or an asserted non-random design (PDF pp. 7-9, sections 4-5; p. 32, Appendix F).

Figure 2 distinguishes a formative study of 12 people, co-design study of 16, and main evaluation of 54: 29 chatbot-companion and 25 medical-AI participants. Each use-case set separately contains fewer than 50 people; the main-evaluation total is 54 (PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and contribution 3).

All recorded workshop headcounts match the printed gender subtotals: S1 = 6, 6; S2 = 5, 6, 5; S3, in form order = 5, 4, 5, 4, 6, 5, 6, 5, 7, 7. Age, education, and AI-expertise subtotals agree with these headcounts; they are workshop participants, not assignment counts (PDF p. 26, Appendix D, Table 9).

Participants could attend only one workshop. The mixed university/company recruitment and separate participant sets are supported; randomized headcounts are not reported (PDF pp. 7-8, section 4, Participants).

The paper says five expert annotators from a pool of 90 rated each impact from all 15 workshops. Raters and generated impacts must not be counted as brainstorming participants; the form correctly flags that the exact workshop subset entering Table 4 models is not separately stated (PDF p. 10, sections 5.1-5.2).

Every printed novelty mean, SE, and significance mark in S3-O1 matches Table 4A. The form correctly preserves the conflict between starred chatbot-benefit novelty cells and the prose claim of no creativity improvement (PDF p. 10, Table 2; p. 11, Table 4A; p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1).
Every printed plausibility mean, SE, and significance mark in S3-O2 matches Table 4A, including the differently starred chatbot-benefit AI and No AI cells (PDF p. 11, Table 4A).

S3-O3 correctly copies impact counts: chatbot benefits 68 versus 29, risks 96 versus 80, mitigations 78 versus 54; medical benefits 33 versus 27, risks 46 versus 42, mitigations 59 versus 29. These count outputs, not people (PDF p. 11, Table 4A, Count).

The prose literally reports 48% more chatbot impacts and 22% more medical impacts. The form appropriately preserves these printed percentages and flags the unexplained medical percentage rather than calculating a replacement effect (PDF p. 12, section 5.3, Finding 1).

Table 4 values are CLM estimated marginal means ± SE, back-transformed to Likert values with Tukey adjustment; they are not standardized effect sizes or means ± SD (PDF pp. 10-11, section 5.2 and Table 4 caption).

The one-line finding accurately quotes chatbot-risk plausibility 3.86 ±.10 versus 3.56 ±.05 and novelty 1.83 ±.11 versus 1.80 ±.03, with limited medical-task gains and unstated randomization (PDF p. 11, Table 4A; p. 12, section 5.3; p. 8, section 4).

The tool is Miro-embedded, uses GPT-4.1, and the Final AI prompt appendix specifies gpt-4.1-2025-04-14 plus gpt-4o-mini-search-preview-2025-03-11 for Related AI Incidents (PDF p. 8, section 4; p. 27, Appendix E).

The recorded durations are supported: formative/co-design workshops lasted 1 hour 45 minutes; Figure 2 specifies 80 minutes of brainstorming, split into 45 minutes ideate, 15 converge, and 20 decide (PDF p. 7, Study setup; p. 3, Figure 2).

The paper reports primary workshop evaluations and ancillary literature mapping, not pooled meta-analytic estimates; empty synthesis-effect defaults are appropriate (PDF pp. 7-12, sections 4-5; pp. 21-22, Appendix A, Tables 5-6).
summary: The 54-person main evaluation does not document random assignment, and its recorded participant counts and reported statistics match the PDF. Corrections concern omitted output ratings, unrecorded supplementary semantic-distance results, and incorrectly denied company involvement.
